title: The Most Compelling Reason to Get Phones Out of Schools
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Martinko argues that the strongest case for bell-to-bell phone bans is one adults almost never make, because it is not about distraction or online safety but about relief from constant surveillance by peers. Her evidence is a Michigan student's testimony to her superintendent that she once spent over an hour getting ready each morning because a classmate might photograph her at any moment, and that the ban returned her ability to be natural. Martinko's diagnosis is generational: adults writing these policies never attended school under the threat of spontaneous documentation and would struggle to find a single high school photograph of themselves. She then widens the frame, drawing on Cal Newport's notion of supercharged socializing and on Kathryn Jezer-Morton's account of carnival rituals, from nineteenth-century shivarees to Brazilian Carnaval, to argue that humans need permissible transgression and that cameras foreclose it. She notes the two available responses to being filmed, avoidance and performance, and points out that both produce the same loss of release, with the modern wedding offered as a carnival of respectability. The conclusion returns to children and reframes the ban as protecting a right rather than imposing a restriction.
points: The argument's originality lies in centring student self-presentation rather than academic distraction or online safety, which Martinko says is where adult policymakers stop.
The Michigan student's account is the load-bearing evidence, and its detail is specific, over an hour of preparation driven by the unpredictability of when a phone would appear.
Martinko links surveillance to a loss of goofiness, citing children now reluctant to be silly or to try new things in case it is filmed.
Newport's supercharged socializing and Jezer-Morton's carnival rituals are used to argue that high-intensity, role-flipping social settings are a human requirement, not a luxury.
She observes that avoidance and reputation-seeking performance converge on the same outcome, since both prevent the catharsis a genuine party provides.
quotes: In the fiery debate over bell-to-bell phone bans in schools, there is one perspective that is rarely considered—and that is how the students themselves feel when they’re no longer at risk of being photographed or filmed every moment of the day.

All of my friends had phones, and I just never knew when one of them was going to whip out their phone in class, in the hallway, or in the bathroom, and take a picture. I felt a constant, daily pressure to look pretty in the pictures.

The fact is that we adults, who are making policies and decisions relating to the presence of smartphones in schools, are thinking more about online safety and distraction than the implications for kids’ self-presentation.

I’ve read about children who are now hesitant to act goofy or silly or even try new things because it might be caught on camera. That is tragic, because goofing off is one of the most beautiful qualities of childhood.

Carnival rituals allowed people to admit and celebrate taboos—bodies, profanity, and the fundamentally arbitrary nature of social hierarchies themselves. Group therapy through permissible transgression, if you will.
We are savvy beings. In the presence of cameras, we adjust our behaviour to mitigate social harm and enhance our reputations, but that is no way to live every minute of every day.
Unless you are some kind of celebrity or politician who has signed up for life in the public eye, you should not have to embark on each new day with a lurking fear of amateur paparazzi.
Put that way, a phone ban doesn’t seem drastic or unrealistic at all. It just sounds like common sense.
